title: Hero
text: Heading. This is the page’s only <h1>. Three <span class="block"> children, not concatenated text nodes.

title: Hero
text: Keyword. Head term rubber components manufacturer India split across H1 (“Precision Rubber Components” + “Manufactured in India”) and resolved literally in the subhead’s first clause. Density in the first 100 words: 2.1%.

title: Hero
text: Entity definition. Subhead opens [Entity] is a [category] in [location] that [does X] — the copula is what makes this liftable by an assistant. Never open with “We”.

title: Hero
text: Internal links. Four in-subhead product links + five industry chips = 9 descriptive outbound links from the hero. No “click here”.

title: Hero
text: LCP image. fetchpriority="high" loading="eager" decoding="async" on the hero background only; every other image on the page loading="lazy". Preload with imagesrcset.

title: Hero
text: Alt text. alt="Margo Rubber Products precision rubber component manufacturing plant in Nashik, India". The circuit overlay gets alt="".

title: Hero
text: Schema. No section-level block. The hero image registers as ImageObject @id=#hero-image, referenced by WebPage.primaryImageOfPage.

title: Hero
text: Certification claim. ISO 9001:2015 only, in the eyebrow and in the fourth stat card. IATF 16949 is not yet held and is deliberately not stated here — the live build claims it outright on /why-margo and /products while /certifications denies it one click away, which is indefensible in front of a procurement auditor and, per the AI-citation audit, risks silent removal from an answer set.

title: Client strip
text: AEO. Named, checkable customers are the strongest citation signal on the page. Generic logo walls are ignored; a named account list is quotable. At 24 names across seven sectors this becomes the page’s answer to “who does Margo actually supply?” — a question no competitor in the Indian SERP answers with names.

title: Client strip
text: Marquee crawlability. All 24 names must be real text in the DOM at first paint, not injected by script and not duplicated for the scroll loop. If the animation needs a cloned track, mark the clone aria-hidden="true" and keep it out of the text layer — a doubled list reads to an extraction pass as 48 customers.

title: Our story
text: Heading. First <h2> on the page. Two <span class="block"> children.

title: Our story
text: Answer block. Paragraph 1’s first sentence is the 40–60 word extractable answer to “who manufactures precision rubber components in Nashik, India?” — entity named, category stated, location stated, date stated, all in one sentence.

title: Our story
text: Internal links. Three: /about (CTA), /certifications (from the ISO badge), /products (from “moulded rubber components”).

title: Our story
text: Schema. No new node. Every figure here must match the Organization node — foundingDate 2005, addressLocality Nashik. A mismatch between prose and schema is worse than omitting the schema.

title: Our story
text: Image. Certificate thumbnail: alt="ISO 9001:2015 certificate 09111526A issued to Margo Rubber Products by Integral Certification Ltd", loading="lazy". The certificate itself still carries the old B-12 MIDC Ambad address — do not publish the scan until that is reconciled with the site NAP.

title: Our story
text: GEO. “Nashik, Maharashtra” appears in prose here, not only in decorative eyebrow markup — that is the check the live build fails.

title: Our story
text: Delivered volume beats account count. “24 named accounts” is true and reads small; 17.9M components a year is the same fact expressed as capability, and it is the figure a procurement buyer sizing a supplier actually needs. Keep the 24 names in section 02 where they are evidence, not a headline.

title: Our story
text: Stat de-duplication. No figure repeats between the hero, this section and section 11. A number shown three times on one page reads as padding to a buyer and adds nothing extractable for an assistant — the live build repeats 27+ and 150+ in all three places.

title: Competitive edge

title: Competitive edge
text: Answer blocks. Cards 3 and 5 are the two most citable passages on the page — “how fast does an Indian rubber manufacturer quote?” and “what monthly volume can they take?”. Both carry a number and a unit in the first clause.

title: Competitive edge

title: Competitive edge

title: Competitive edge

title: Sectors we serve

title: How we work
text: This is the highest-value AEO section on the page. Four of the buyer questions in the fan-out map resolve here: how is a custom part quoted, how fast is a prototype, what is the lead time, can you reverse-engineer without a drawing. Each answer sits in its own step with a number in it.

title: Our facility

title: Our facility

title: Our facility

title: Our facility
text: Images. Plant photography, loading="lazy". Alt pattern: alt="Automated compression moulding press at the Margo Rubber Products plant, Nashik". One geo-bearing alt per image, not the same string repeated.

title: Our facility
text: GEO. Coordinates are confirmed and unused — the live build emits neither them nor a Google Business Profile at the same NAP. Together they are the cheapest local-signal upgrade available.

title: Export markets
text: This section fixes the site’s worst structural defect. /export currently has zero inbound links from any header, footer or body on any page — the strongest page on a site named margo-rubber-export is reachable only by typing the URL. This footnote link is its first.

title: Export markets
text: Anchor targets. Live /export jump links emit as /#australia instead of /export#australia, so every market link lands on the homepage. Cards here must link /export#australia, /export#uk, /export#uae-saudi, /export#malaysia — root-relative anchors are the bug, fix at source.

title: Export markets
text: Heading levels. <h2> + four <h3> market names. Country codes are <span aria-hidden="true">; the accessible name is the full country.

title: Export markets
text: Map. Inline SVG, not an image — the country labels must be in the text layer for a crawler and an LLM to read. <title> and <desc> on the <svg>, role="img".

title: Export markets
text: GEO. Ports and transit days are the strongest generative-engine signal on the page — they are checkable, specific, and no Indian competitor publishes them. Keep the number ranges; drop them and this section scores 60.

title: Export markets
text: Schema. areaServed on the Organization contactPoint carries the country list. Do not create a second geo node here.

title: Export markets
text: Vision-build guard. On the buyer-facing build this H2 becomes “Where we are opening lanes first” and every card reads as a target market, not an active one.

title: Material engineering
text: The most citable block on the site. Eight compounds with numeric ranges and named test standards is exactly the passage shape an LLM lifts. No competitor in the Indian SERP publishes it.

title: Material engineering
text: Markup. A real <table> with <caption> and <th scope="col">, visually styled as bars. Do not build it from <div>s — the tabular relationship is what makes it extractable.

title: Material engineering
text: Heading levels. <h2> only. Compound names are <th scope="row">, not <h3>.

title: Material engineering
text: Internal links. AEM → /industries/automotive, FKM → /products/oil-seals#fkm, silicone → /industries/medical-devices, EPDM → /products/sponge-foam-rubber. Four, on the compound names.

title: Material engineering

title: Material engineering

Every <label for> bound to its input; autocomplete="organization | country-name | email | tel"; required on the four starred fields; type="email" and type="tel"; enctype="multipart/form-data" on the file field with accept=".pdf,.dwg,.dxf,image/*". Error text names the field and the fix, never “invalid input”.

title: Footer

title: Hero

title: Hero
text: Keyword. Head term custom rubber parts manufacturer sits in H1 line 1 + subhead. Secondary rubber components manufacturer India resolves in the subhead’s first clause. First-100-word density 2.3%.

title: Hero

title: Hero
text: Internal links. Two in-page anchors (#range, #catalogue) plus the breadcrumb. Anchors must be /products#range, not /#range — the root-relative anchor bug that breaks all eight jump links on /export is the same component.

title: Hero

title: Product range

text: Filter must not hide content from crawlers. All 11 cards render in the DOM at first paint; the filter chips toggle CSS classes, not React conditional rendering. If cards unmount, ten of eleven category links disappear from the crawlable page.

product name inside the ; overline is a

title: Product range

title: Manufacturing excellence

title: Manufacturing excellence

title: Manufacturing excellence

text: Why the tolerance claim matters more than it looks. Publishing ±0.01 mm on moulded rubber tells a specifying engineer the page was not written by someone who moulds rubber. It costs more credibility than the four fabricated stats above it, because it is the one an expert catches instantly.

title: Manufacturing process

title: Material expertise
text: Tab accessibility and crawlability. role="tablist" / role="tab" / role="tabpanel", aria-selected, arrow-key navigation. All eight panels must be in the DOM with inactive ones hidden by CSS, not unmounted — seven of eight compound descriptions vanish from the crawlable page otherwise, and this is the passage an LLM most wants to lift.

title: Material expertise
text: Deep-linkable tabs. /products#aem, #fkm, #silicone … so the compound table on the homepage and the FKM oil-seal resource article can link straight to a panel. Canonical stays /products.

section,

compound name inside each panel. The full polymer name is a

title: Material expertise
text: Consistency gate. These eight ranges must match the homepage table and every category page character for character. FKM currently publishes at three different ranges across the live site; −20 °C to +250 °C is the single source.

title: Material expertise
text: Compound ranges are governed by one table. The eight values here match the homepage compound table exactly, which is the single source for the whole site. Two carry an open question — FKM at 250 °C is above the 200–210 °C industry continuous rating and reads as a peak, and AEM at 175 °C is an advanced-grade figure. Both are flagged in sheet 01 section 10; settle them there and the change propagates to all eleven category pages.

title: Material expertise

title: Industries we serve
text: Nine panels in the DOM, CSS-hidden. Same rule as section 05. These nine passages are the product↔industry crossover content — the highest-value thing on a hub page — and unmounting eight of nine deletes them from the crawl.

title: Industries we serve
text: Nine internal links out, one per panel, to /industries/{slug}. Anchor text is “Rubber components for {sector}”, not “Find {sector} Solutions”.

title: Industries we serve
text: Products-supplied field links too. Each named product in that field links to its category page — roughly 27 additional contextual links, product to industry, which is the internal-linking pattern the whole architecture was designed around and which the live build does not implement anywhere.

title: Industries we serve
text: Slug display map. Tab labels are display names; the live build interpolates raw slugs into prose elsewhere (“Available to hvac buyers”). Never render the slug.

title: Industries we serve
text: Honest negatives stay. ISO 13485 and NORSOK non-claims are load-bearing — they are what makes the rest of the panel credible.

title: Industries we serve
text: Named clients are the strongest field in this section. A sector panel that names Mahindra & Mahindra, IDEX or Starlite Lighting answers “who do they actually supply in my industry?” — a question none of the seven Indian competitors in the teardown answers anywhere on their sites. Trade mark line required beneath the tab set, verbatim: Trade marks shown are the property of their respective owners and appear solely to identify commercial supply relationships. Logo use needs written permission per account; text wordmarks until it lands.

title: Industries we serve
text: Schema. None. Each /industries/* page owns its own node; duplicating them here splits the entity.

title: Certifications
text: The live section, unchanged, caps the whole page at 60. A single fabricated claim caps a section regardless of everything else, and four claims here are contradicted by another page on the same domain — not merely unsourced, but actively refuted one click away. Putting the status inside the badge lifts the cap, because an accurate statement about a future certification is not a false statement about a present one.

title: Certifications
text: Why publish the roadmap at all. A buyer already in conversation, and an assistant asked “is Margo working towards IATF?”, both get a clear answer with a timeframe instead of silence. The bracketed status keeps the two questions separate — what is held today, and what is coming — without ever presenting the second as the first.

title: Certifications
text: Why it is worse than a ranking problem. Per the AI-citation audit, an assistant that finds a certification claimed flatly on one page and denied on another resolves the conflict by dropping the source, not by picking one. That is why every status now reads identically on all four pages that carry one. An overclaim risks silent removal from the answer set — strictly worse than having said nothing.

title: Certifications
text: Schema. Only the ISO 9001:2015 row goes in hasCredential, and only on the homepage Organization node. No In Progress row is emitted as structured data in any form — there is no schema.org property for “certification we are working towards”, and forcing one into hasCredential, award or knowsAbout makes a machine read it as held. In Progress rows are visible text only.

title: Certifications
text:
Heading levels.

+ five

card titles. The status bracket is part of the badge

, not the heading — a heading reading “IATF 16949:2016 (In Progress)” puts the caveat into the document outline, where an extraction pass may drop the parenthetical and keep the claim.

title: Certifications
text: Badge images. Do not use ISO or IATF logo marks. Certification body logos are trademark-controlled and their use is licensed by the certificate; a text badge carries the same information with none of the exposure.

title: Certifications
text: Procurement reality. A buyer’s first act after reading this section is to ask for the certificate PDF. Ship the scope and number in the copy so the request confirms rather than contradicts.

title: In-house testing
text: Two named groups outrank one long list. A buyer scanning for “do they test ozone in-house?” gets a direct answer. An assistant asked the same question gets a passage with a subject, a standard number and a boundary — all three checkable.

title: In-house testing
text: Markup. Two <table>s with <caption>, not chip <div>s. Test name and standard are a key–value relationship and the table is what makes it extractable.

title: In-house testing
text: Heading levels. <h2> + two <h3> group headings.

title: In-house testing
text: Standard numbers are citation bait. Twelve ASTM and ISO designations on one page is a stronger authority signal for this query class than any amount of adjective copy, and no competitor in the Indian SERP publishes them.

title: In-house testing
text: Gated PDF. If the capability statement ships, serve it from a real URL rather than an email-gated modal, and let it be crawled — a linkable technical PDF earns citations that a gated one never will.

title: Catalogue download
text: A gated PDF earns nothing. It cannot be crawled, cannot be cited, cannot rank and cannot be lifted into an AI answer. Every technical table inside it is content Margo already owns and is choosing not to publish.

title: Catalogue download
text: If ungated: serve from /downloads/margo-product-catalogue-2026.pdf, link it from this section, the footer and every category page, and add <meta name="robots" content="index, follow"> equivalent via X-Robots-Tag. Set the PDF’s own /Title metadata — it becomes the SERP title.

title: Catalogue download
text: Form. Three <label for> bindings, autocomplete="name | email | organization", type="email". Consent checkbox required under DPDP if the address is used for anything beyond sending the file — and the copy must say which.

title: Catalogue download
text: Schema. Optional DigitalDocument with encodingFormat: "application/pdf" and datePublished. Only worth shipping if the file is ungated.

title: Catalogue download
text: Heading levels. <h2> + <h3> on “Get instant access”. The ▤ glyph used as a decorative icon needs aria-hidden="true".

title: FAQ
text: Question phrasing. Every question is written the way a buyer types it, taken from the fan-out enumeration, not the way a marketer would phrase it. “What if we have no drawing?” is a real search; “Can you manufacture to customer drawings and specifications?” is a brochure sentence.

title: FAQ
text: Answer length. 40–60 words is the passage window assistants lift. All eight sit inside it. Each opens with the answer, not with a restatement of the question.

title: FAQ
text: Markup. <details>/<summary> or a button-driven accordion with aria-expanded and aria-controls. All eight answers in the DOM regardless of open state — a collapsed answer is still crawlable, an unmounted one is not.

title: FAQ
text: Heading levels. <h2> + eight <h3> question headings inside the summary elements.

title: FAQ
text: Schema. The FAQPage node in the page-level block carries these eight pairs verbatim. Text in the JSON-LD and text on the page must match exactly — a mismatch is a structured-data violation.

title: FAQ
text: MOQ. The live Q1 states “typically 100 pieces” and “generally 500 to 1,000 pieces” in one answer, and the page elsewhere says 500. Standing founder instruction, 2026-08-19: never publish a piece count, never claim to take only big orders, quote by part size. This answer is where it leaks most visibly.

title: FAQ
text: Internal links. Six, inside the answers — /products/o-rings, #compounds, /certifications, /export, /contact, /about#plant.

title: Request a quote
text: NAP consistency. Phone, email and address must match the homepage Organization node and the footer character for character. title: Factory vs trading company
text: This is a genuine AEO passage. “How do I tell a rubber manufacturer from a trading company?” is a real buyer question with almost no honest published answers, and three structural tests — who mixes, who owns the tooling, who signs the batch — is exactly the shape an answer engine lifts.
